title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Runbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical playbook for Redwood Inference's serving runtime: high-level architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes for recent runtime changes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers (runtime, infra, SRE), oncall responders, and release owners.

High-level goals:
- Provide a predictable, low-latency, high-throughput inference runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Enable safe rollouts with measurable performance and quality guardrails.
- Provide standardized profiling and benchmarking so teams can compare kernels, quantization profiles, and model variants.

Scope:
- Runtime service components (runtime-service, scheduler, kv-cache, batch-manager)
- Kernel selection and scheduling policies for GPU/CPU/ML accelerators
- Profiling procedures and artifacts to collect for perf triage
- Benchmarking suite usage and expected baselines
- Runbooks for common incidents and escalation paths

1) Architecture overview

1.1 Components (logical)
- runtime-service: API front-end, request validation, auth, request routing.
- batch-manager: groups compatible requests into batches, manages timeouts and max batch sizes.
- scheduler: maps batches to worker pods/nodes and selects execution kernels (CUDA/cuBLAS/TensorCore/ROCm/ML-optimized kernels).
- worker (inference-worker): runs model execution, manages KV cache, executes kernels, handles streaming output.
- kv-cache: LRU cache for KV-prefix state used by autoregressive sampling. Shared per-customer scope when configured.
- metrics-exporter: emits Prometheus metrics and traces (OpenTelemetry).

1.2 Data plane flow
1. API request hits runtime-service -> validation & tenant fetch.
2. batch-manager evaluates request compatibility (model id, quantization, sequence length, sampling params).
3. scheduler selects target worker pool and kernel variant via kernel-profile table.
4. worker executes; partial outputs stream back via runtime-service to client.
5. metrics, traces, and prof events are exported asynchronously.

1.3 SLOs and safety thresholds (production defaults)
- 99th percentile latency (text generation, seq_len=1024): <= 350ms for hosted tier default models.
- 95th percentile latency (embeddings): <= 50ms.
- Error budget target: <= 0.1% 5xx across all requests per rolling 7d window.
- Maximum batching latency budget (per-batch delay): 30ms default, configurable per-route.

2) Kernel selection & scheduling design

2.1 Kernel-profile table
- Kernel profiles are precomputed per model-family, sequence length buckets, and hardware type. Keys: model-family | quantization | seq_bucket | hw_target -> preferred_kernel, fallback_kernels, expected_throughput_tps, expected_latency_ms.
- Profiles are stored in the model-catalog and surfaced to scheduler at runtime.

2.2 Scheduling policies (priority order)
1. Hard affinity: tenant pinned to dedicated pool -> respect pin.
2. Latency-first: route to low-latency kernel variant (smaller batch sizes, optimized TensorCore kernels).
3. Cost-first: higher batching to improve tokens-per-dollar for non-latency critical routes.
4. Fallback policy: if preferred kernel fails or resources constrained, fall back to compatible kernel variants or lower-precision quantized kernels.

2.3 Runtime heuristics and protections
- Batch size caps by model and hw to prevent OOM.
- KV cache throttling: limit cached prefixes per-tenant to avoid memory pressure.
- Slow-kernel gating: scheduler demotes kernels with sustained 95th percentile degradation (>30% above baseline) and triggers a rollout alert.

3) Profiling playbook (how to collect actionable perf data)

3.1 When to profile
- New model onboarding (first 3 deployments).
- Post-rollback investigations after performance regressions.
- Before enabling new quantization profile or kernel.

3.2 Artifacts to collect (minimum set)
- Prometheus metrics window (5m before, during, and 5m after test): request_latency_histogram, batch_sizes, gpu_mem_usage_bytes, cpu_usage_percent, nvlink_bandwidth.
- Flamegraphs of worker process (sampling profiler, 30s baseline + 60s stress).
- Kernel timers: per-op execution times exported by our kernel instrumentation layer.
- Full distributed trace (OpenTelemetry) for sampled requests including batch-manager -> scheduler -> worker spans.
- Representative request payloads and sequence lengths used.
- Model binary checksum and kernel-profile used.

3.3 Profiling procedure (step-by-step)
1. Create a dedicated profiling job in the qa-namespace to avoid noisy neighbors.
2. Reproduce workload with load generator: use bench-client --model <model> --seq 1024 --qps 20 --sampling top_p=0.9 (see bench commands below).
3. Enable kernel timers and verbose tracing for the run (config flag: runtime.profile.kernels=true).
4. Collect metrics and flamegraphs; annotate with model_id, kernel_profile, hw_target.
5. Analyze: identify top 3 latency contributors (>5% of total). If kernel-bound, capture per-op breakdown to determine if fusion or alternative kernel yields improvement.

Example bench commands:
- bench-client --target runtime-service.internal:443 --model gptx-13b --seq 1024 --qps 10 --duration 300s --concurrency 16
- bench-client --target runtime-service.internal:443 --model longform-6b-ql --seq 2048 --qps 5 --client-profiling

3.4 Success criteria for kernel change
- 95th perc latency improvement >= 10% OR tokens/sec improvement >= 15% without increasing 5xx.
- GPU memory delta within safe margin (+/- 5%).
- No increase in decoding errors or quality regressions per eval harness.

4) Benchmarking suite (how we run controlled benchmarks)

4.1 Bench categories
- Microbenchmarks: single-op, transformer-block, KV cache hit/miss latency.
- Model-level benchmarks: end-to-end generation with representative prompts.
- Cost-bench: tokens-per-second and cost-per-token estimates across quantization options.

4.2 Reproducible workflow
1. Use infra-scripts/bench/deploy-benchmark with pinned AMI and kernel build id.
2. Use bench-config YAML with the following fields (example):
    model: gptx-13b
    seq_lengths: [128,512,1024]
    qps: [1,5,10]
    runtime_flags: ["--kernel-profile=opt-v3","--kv-cache-policy=shared"]
3. Capture artifacts to s3://redwood-bench/<run_id>/ including metrics, logs, and flamegraphs.
4. Results are uploaded to the Bench UI and compared against baseline runs; diffs above thresholds auto-create a regression ticket.

4.3 Baseline expectations (example)
- gptx-13b fp16, seq=1024, single-GPU: 1200 tokens/sec (\u00b110%).
- gptx-6b int4, seq=512, single-GPU: 2500 tokens/sec (\u00b112%).

5) Release notes (runtime v2026-02)*

Summary of changes (v2026-02):
- Kernel selection: introduced "latency-first" kernel variant that defaults for hosted-latency tier routes. Expected 95p latency reduction of 18% on gptx-13b on A100-80GB.
- Batch-manager: new adaptive batching heuristic that reduces tail latency for bursty traffic (config flag runtime.batch.adaptive=true).
- Monitoring: added kernel-level timers to metrics export (metric name: runtime_kernel_op_ms).
- Stability: fixed mem-leak in kv-cache eviction logic that affected high-concurrency tenants.

Rollout plan:
1. Canary 5% on hosted cluster (2026-02-08) - monitor kernel success rate and 95p latency.
2. Expand to 25% (2026-02-12) - verify cost heuristics.
3. Full rollout to hosted and dedicated kernels (2026-02-20).

Known impact notes: the latency-first variant increases small-batch GPU utilization; we observed ~4% higher cost for high-throughput, non-latency workloads. If cost sensitive, set policy cost-first.

6) Known issues (current as of last_updated)

- Issue: Intermittent 5xx during adaptive batching under bursty ingress (tracker: RUNTIME-872).
  - Symptoms: short spikes of 5xx for ~2-10s, correlated with large queue depth.
  - Workaround: set runtime.batch.adaptive=false on route until fix is deployed.
  - Status: partial fix merged (2026-02-25), full mitigation targeted for 2026-03-10.

- Issue: OOMs when using int4 quantization on models with dynamic-length attention (tracker: RUNTIME-903).
  - Symptoms: worker pod OOMKilled during long sequence generations > 4096 tokens.
  - Workaround: pin quantization to int8 for long-seq routes or increase worker GPU memory class.
  - Status: investigating; short-term kernel patch planned.

- Issue: KV cache eviction race in heavy multi-tenant mode (resolved)
  - Note: was root-caused and fixed in v2026-02; older releases still affected.

7) Operational runbooks (incident playbooks)

7.1 High 95th percentile latency (alert: runtime.high_95_latency)
1. Acknowledge and assign: oncall SRE + runtime-owner.
2. Check service health dashboards: per-route latency, batch sizes, kernel success rates.
3. Run quick diagnostics:
   - kubectl exec into sample worker pod and check GPU utilization: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv
   - curl runtime-service/health and runtime-service/metrics?service=kernel
4. If kernel success rate < 99%: roll back to previous kernel-profile via model-catalog flag.
5. If batches growing and queue depth high: temporarily lower batch.delay_ms to 10ms and enable per-route max_batch_size=1 for critical routes.
6. Create post-incident ticket and attach profiling artifacts.

7.2 5xx spike across region (alert: runtime.bulk_5xx)
1. Verify upstream ingress and auth (API gateway logs).
2. Check worker OOMs and pod restarts: kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide | grep OOMKilled.
3. If many pods OOMKilled, scale up node pool or drain problematic nodes.
4. If persistent after scaling, trigger rollback to previous runtime release.

Runbook commands (quick)
- kubectl -n runtime logs deploy/runtime-service --since=10m | grep ERROR | tail -n 200
- bench-client --target runtime-service.internal:443 --model <model> --seq 1024 --qps 1 --duration 60s --capture-trace=./trace.json

9) Appendix: example config table

Config key | Default | Description
---------- | ------- | -----------
runtime.batch.max_size | 64 | Max requests per batch by default.
runtime.batch.delay_ms | 30 | Max wait to form a batch before dispatch.
runtime.scheduler.policy | latency-first | Default scheduling policy for hosted-latency tier.
runtime.profile.kernels | false | Enable verbose kernel timing export.

If you are making an operational change (kernel, batch policy, or quantization profile), follow the rollout checklist in section 2 of this document and notify runtime-owner and SRE channels before canarying.
